summary: QA-800 is the Fe–9Mn–5Al–0.3C (wt.%) low-density δ-TRIP steel plate state obtained by intercritical quenching at 1050 °C for 1 h (water quench) followed by intercritical annealing at 800 °C for 1 h and air cooling. It retains the micro-laminated δ-ferrite band / tempered martensite lamellar structure of the hot-rolled precursor, but after this highest annealing temperature a large fraction of fine austenite (~48 % by XRD, ~49 % by EBSD) is dispersed in the tempered martensite region, and part of the austenite is so unstable that newly formed martensite appears already during air cooling. The sample is one of four quenched-and-annealed (QA-620/680/740/800) states used to study how annealing temperature controls austenite stability, TRIP/TWIP activity and the strength–ductility balance of the steel.
composition: The alloy is a medium-Mn, Al-bearing low-density steel designated Fe–9Mn–5Al-0.3C (wt.%). The analysed chemical composition (Table 1, wt.%) is C 0.29, Al 4.6, Mn 8.9, P < 0.005, S < 0.005, Fe balance — consistent with the nominal designation. It was prepared as a 5 kg ingot in a vacuum induction furnace, with the very low P and S contents reflecting impurity control. The Al addition (4.6 wt.%) is the source of the low density — measured 7.34 g·cm⁻³ by the Archimedes drainage method, i.e. 6.7 % lower than low-carbon low-alloy steels — and it also expands the δ-ferrite phase field so that the steel cannot be fully austenitized, producing the δ-ferrite + austenite dual-phase window exploited by the heat treatment. Mn (8.9 wt.%) acts as the austenite stabilizer added together with Al, keeping the Mn level below the ~12 wt.% that is discouraged on grounds of weldability, corrosion resistance, segregation and cost. C at 0.29 wt.% supports austenite stabilization and the TRIP behaviour.
processing: The processing lineage leading to QA-800 is: (1) homogenization of the 5 kg vacuum-induction ingot at 1100 °C for 2 h; (2) forging at 1100 °C into a square forging ingot of 80 mm × 70 mm; (3) reheating to 1100 °C for 2 h, then hot rolling from 80 to 12 mm thickness in eight passes with an initial rolling temperature of ~1050 °C and a finishing rolling temperature of ~950 °C, followed by air cooling to room temperature (state HR); (4) intercritical quenching (IQ) — reheating the hot-rolled plate to 1050 °C, in the ferrite + austenite dual-phase region, for 1 h followed by water quenching (state IQ-1050), which is the parent state of QA-800; and (5) intercritical annealing of the water-quenched plate at 800 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling, giving state QA-800. The 800 °C annealing temperature was selected from Thermo-Calc calculation as the upper end of the 620–800 °C annealing window above the Ac1 = 617 °C cementite-precipitation temperature. Note that the annealing cooling step for QA-800 is air cooling, which is slow enough that part of the unstable austenite transforms to martensite before the tensile test.
microstructure: QA-800 retains the micro-laminated (banded) microstructure inherited from the hot-rolled/IQ states, consisting of elongated coarse δ-ferrite bands (BCC, A2) alternating with tempered martensite lamellar (BCC). After annealing, a large number of fine austenite grains — a mixture of retained austenite from quenching and reverted austenite — are widely distributed in the tempered martensite region, mainly in the martensitic lath gaps. Austenite (FCC, A1) reaches ~48 % by XRD and ~49 % by EBSD; the EBSD map shows large, coarse blocky austenite blocks and bands, the highest visible austenite area fraction among the annealed states. Austenite grain size is fine and its distribution peaks in the <1.6 µm bin (about 30 % or just above), falls monotonically through the intermediate bins with a small secondary rise in the >4.8 µm bin (below 10 %), so that about 90 % of austenite grains are smaller than 4.8 µm. A distinctive feature of QA-800 is newly formed martensite (BCC) inside the tempered martensite region, produced from austenite by martensitic transformation during air cooling of the annealed plate (highlighted in the red box of Fig. 3(h)). Geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities are 4.63 ×10¹⁴ m⁻² for the BCC phase and 2.66 ×10¹⁴ m⁻² for the FCC phase — the lowest of all investigated states. The tempered martensite shows a coarse lath/blocky morphology with low band contrast; KAM maps are almost uniformly dark blue (lowest residual misorientation of the series) and the grain-boundary network is very sparse, with austenitic grain (AG) boundaries (15°–45°) prevailing while block boundaries (>45°) decrease continuously with annealing temperature, and low-angle packet and sub-block boundaries almost absent. δ-ferrite bands remain elongated but deficient in high-angle boundaries.
properties: Mechanical testing was performed at room temperature on an electronic tensile machine WDW-100E at a strain rate of 0.375 min⁻¹, using rod-shaped specimens M10×60 mm with a 25 mm gauge length and the tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction of the hot-rolled plate. QA-800 shows: yield strength 469 ± 4 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 719 ± 10 MPa, total elongation 50.4 ± 3.2 %, yield-to-tensile ratio 0.65 and product of strength and elongation (PSE) 36.2 ± 2.9 GPa%. Its engineering stress–strain curve is the gold curve of Fig. 5(a), with a lower strength plateau (~700–850 MPa) extending to ~50 % strain; in the true stress–strain curve the necking point lies near 0.4 true strain, followed by a near-vertical drop. The work-hardening-rate curve falls steeply from ~8000 MPa near zero strain, plateaus a little above the 1000 MPa gridline with a small rise before necking, and follows the same three-stage (I/II/III) shape as the other QA states. Austenite stability descriptors for QA-800 are k ≈ 1.50 (the highest of the QA series, i.e. the lowest mechanical stability) and SFE ≈ 31.53 mJ·m⁻² (SFP ≈ 5.59 ×10⁻⁴, ε²₅₀ ≈ 9.68 ×10⁻⁵), the lowest SFE of the four QA states but still within the 20–40 mJ·m⁻² window in which TWIP is expected. The tensile fracture surface is a layered mixed-mode fracture: quasi-cleavage at the top, then a dimple band, then a cleavage layer with cleavage steps and a second crack at the bottom. Characterization techniques applied to this steel and state include FE-SEM (MIRA-3 LMH), EBSD (Oxford, HKL Channel5 + Python analysis), XRD (SmartLab, Cu-Kα, 40 kV/150 mA, 0.02° step, 2°/min) with Rietveld refinement (FullProf) for austenite fraction and SFE, KAM-based GND calculation, Thermo-Calc (TCFE 12) equilibrium calculation, and room-temperature tensile testing.
mechanisms: Annealing at the highest temperature (800 °C) makes small austenite grains grow and dilutes the C and Mn in austenite, so the Ms temperature rises and part of the extremely unstable austenite transforms to martensite already during air cooling; this new martensite forms inside the tempered martensite region and lowers the residual austenite fraction of QA-800 below that of QA-740 despite the higher annealing temperature.

The recovery effect of annealing progressively reduces the GND density in tempered martensite and austenite; QA-800 has the lowest martensitic and austenitic GND densities, so dislocation slip starts more easily and the yield strength of the tempered martensite lamellar falls, which is one of the two main causes of the low YS (469 MPa).

The austenite fraction increases with annealing temperature and austenite is a soft phase in which ductile deformation starts preferentially; a larger soft-phase fraction initiates ductile deformation earlier, lowering the yield strength — the second main cause of the YS decrease of the annealed specimens.

Within the grain-boundary network, block boundaries (>45°) decrease continuously with annealing temperature while AG boundaries (15°–45°) increase; because the coarse δ-ferrite grains carry almost no boundaries, boundary effects operate through the martensite, and the loss of block-boundary density contributes further to the drop in yield strength of the annealed states.

With increasing annealing temperature, reverted austenite nucleates and grows at martensite lath gaps with diffusion of C and Mn into austenite and Al into martensite/ferrite, so block boundaries are progressively replaced by austenitic grain boundaries; finer austenite grains retain a higher alloy enrichment and thus higher stability, while coarser grains are less stable.

Low GND density in the tempered martensite promotes coordinated deformation between the tempered martensite lamellae and the δ-ferrite bands, which is beneficial to the plasticity of the steel and helps explain the high elongation of the annealed states.

Austenite stability governs the deformation mechanism: k ≈ 1.50 for QA-800 is the highest (i.e. stability the lowest) of the QA series, so a notable TRIP effect occurs, but because part of the unstable austenite was already consumed by air-cooling martensite, less austenite transforms during deformation than in QA-740, giving lower ductility (50.4 % versus 62.4 % TE).

The estimated SFE of ~31.53 mJ·m⁻² lies between 20 and 40 mJ·m⁻², so TWIP is expected to operate alongside TRIP; k and SFE vary in opposite senses but describe the same stability ranking (lower k = higher SFE = higher stability).

All QA states share a three-stage work-hardening behaviour: stage I is dominated by dislocation gliding in ferrite, austenite and tempered martensite according to phase hardness and by the increased dislocation mean free path in the coarsened δ-ferrite, so WHR falls sharply; stage II is a competition between hardening (grain boundaries, dislocation tangles, TRIP) and softening (dislocation gliding, annihilation, cross-slip); stage III shows a slow WHR rise as TRIP dominates.

In stage II only a few relatively large austenite grains transform, giving weak hardening, whereas in stage III a larger number of small austenite grains reach the critical strain and transform, and the resulting fine hard martensite particles dispersed in the tempered martensite region act both as obstacles to dislocation gliding and as sites of dislocation accumulation, giving a second-phase-particle-like strengthening that sustains the WHR.

During tension, dislocation accumulation at the δ-ferrite/tempered martensite interfaces plus the hardness difference between the two phases promotes stress concentration and crack initiation; the crack is captured by the δ-ferrite and propagates into and along the δ-ferrite band to form second cracks (deep valleys).

Because δ-ferrite is soft, a crack entering it is blunted, producing high resistance to cracking; additionally, strain-induced martensitic transformation causes volume expansion that promotes closure of cracks, both being positive for ductility.

The coarse δ-ferrite has deficient high-angle grain boundaries that cannot effectively hinder microcrack propagation, so cleavage morphology (river patterns, cleavage steps) forms in the δ-ferrite during fracture, consistent with {100} cleavage being the natural BCC failure mode; fracture is a mixed cleavage/quasi-cleavage/dimple mode with laminar tears from the banded structure.

The necking point of QA-800 lies near 0.4 true strain with a near-vertical drop immediately after; among the QA states, ductility and the strain at necking shift to larger strain with increasing annealing temperature up to 740 °C, and the newly formed air-cooling martensite in QA-800 deteriorates ductility relative to QA-740.
conclusions: QA-800 belongs to the family of intercritical-quenched-and-annealed states of the Fe–8.9Mn–4.6Al–0.29C low-density δ-TRIP steel that trade strength for ductility: annealing after quenching raises total elongation from 2.0 % (IQ-1050) to ~50 %, at the cost of lowering yield strength (469 MPa) and tensile strength (719 MPa). It exhibits the highest residual austenite fraction of the series together with the lowest GND densities and the lowest SFE (~31.53 mJ·m⁻²), but its tensile ductility (TE 50.4 %, PSE 36.2 GPa%) is inferior to that of QA-740 (TE 62.4 %, PSE 45.2 GPa%), which has the best strength–ductility balance. The reason is that at 800 °C the austenite grains coarsen and its C, Mn are diluted, raising Ms so that a portion of the austenite transforms to martensite already during air cooling; the resulting new martensite and the reduced amount of austenite available for TRIP during deformation both degrade ductility. Overall, the annealed experimental steel shows wide yield strength grades (460–620 MPa) with excellent ductility and a low yield-to-tensile ratio (0.65 for QA-800), making it a typical third-generation advanced high-strength steel that, with its low density advantage, could substitute for TRIP 580T/400Y (or 590T/400Y) high-strength automobile steel plates.

The austenite volume fractions reported by EBSD and XRD differ slightly (~49 % versus ~48 % for QA-800); the paper notes the discrepancy exists but the trend with annealing temperature is similar and states that subsequent discussion uses the XRD data.
